title: Compositions with Inverse Trig
short: Evaluate expressions like sin⁻¹(sin 5π/6) and cos(tan⁻¹ x).
trouble: Students cancel sin⁻¹(sin θ) to θ even when θ is outside [−π/2, π/2].

blocks.html: A function and its inverse undo each other, but with inverse trig functions that is only half true, because of the restricted ranges. This lesson sorts out which way works and how to handle the other.

$\sin(\arcsin x) = x$ for every $x$ in $[-1, 1]$. But $\arcsin(\sin\theta) = \theta$ only when $\theta$ is in $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$; otherwise it is the angle in that range with the same sine. The same goes for cosine (range $[0, \pi]$) and tangent. For expressions like $\cos(\arctan x)$, name the angle and draw a right triangle.

$\arcsin x$ is an angle whose sine is $x$, so taking its sine gives back $x$. Going the other way, $\sin\theta$ forgets which angle it came from: $\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}$ and $\sin\frac{\pi}{6}$ are both $\frac{1}{2}$. Arcsine can only answer with the angle in its range.

blocks.name: unitcircle
blocks.cap: At $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ the height is the same as at $\frac{\pi}{6}$. Arcsine returns the one on the right half of the circle.

blocks.title: A triangle
steps: Let $\theta = \arctan\frac{3}{4}$, so $\tan\theta = \frac{3}{4}$ and $\theta$ is in Quadrant I.
Draw a right triangle with opposite side $3$ and adjacent side $4$; the hypotenuse is $5$.

blocks.title: Watch the quadrant
steps: Let $\theta = \arccos\left(-\frac{5}{13}\right)$. It is in $[0, \pi]$ with a negative cosine, so it is in Quadrant II.
Sine is positive in Quadrant II: $\sin\theta = \frac{12}{13}$.

blocks.title: With a variable
steps: Let $\theta = \arctan x$, so $\tan\theta = \frac{x}{1}$: opposite $x$, adjacent $1$, hypotenuse $\sqrt{1 + x^2}$.
$\cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + x^2}}$. On $\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ cosine is positive, so this works for negative $x$ too.

blocks.html: Cancelling $\arcsin(\sin\theta)$ to $\theta$ every time. Check the answer against the range: an arcsine can never be $\frac{5\pi}{6}$, and an arccosine can never be negative.
